newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Tutsis displace Hutus in Zaire civil war.
newsitem.headline: Tutsis displace Hutus in Zaire civil war.

text.p: Far behind the lines of an advance by Zaire rebels, a "dirty war" between Rwandan Hutu militias and Tutsi rebels is changing the ethnic balance of eastern Zaire.
Tutsi herdsmen moving back with their cattle to the Mushaki district 35 km (22 miles) west of Goma say Hutu farmers who also lived there had either fled or been killed by rebel troops.

"The Hutus who were here have all gone, and it's true that some of them were killed. All the Hutus here were part of the same plot," said Rubayazi Gwanamisa, a Zairean Tutsi herdsman who had just brought his cattle from neighbouring Rwanda.

Since launching their rebellion in October to topple Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko, the rebels have occupied about a quarter of the vast country where Hutus and Tutsis are tiny minorities among over 200 tribes.

The rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire has consistently denied accusations of human rights abuses and systematic killings of Hutus by the ethnic Tutsi core of its fighting force.

Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army denies that its troops are in Zaire, but some rebel fighters say they took part in the war that ended Rwanda's 1994 genocide of an estimated 800,000 minority Tutsis and Hutu moderates.
Rwanda's army stands to gain if it can secure East Zaire from the threat of militant Hutus, diplomats say, and the Tutsi herdsmen say they want more land for their cattle.
Members of the Hutu Interahamwe ("We who stand together") militias and former Rwandan army are blamed for the genocide.

They took to the hills west of Goma after the rebels overran their refugee camps in eastern Zaire last year, and found shelter among Zairean Hutu villagers who have now been forced deeper into the hills by the fighting.
Huddled in a bar over bottles of frothy banana beer, a group of Tutsi herdsmen, some recently returned from Rwanda, sheltered from the rain that feeds the lush pastures of Mushaki.
"The liberators are here to make sure the Interahamwe can never return and we can live in peace," said Munya Kabuga.
Local Tutsis said that many Hutus were killed during fighting in January and February, and few Hutus now remained in the village.
"When they found them (the Hutus) they shot them, they had done wrong and many of them were armed, hundreds of them were killed by the liberators," said Umfonzi Kabuye.
"But not all the Hutus were bad -- and those who know they did nothing wrong are welcome to return."

While there is no longer fighting in Mushaki, travellers say the war is still intense in nearby areas. They report seeing at least 10 bodies beside the road at the village of Kisuma, 20 km (12 miles) from Mushaki, on Friday.
Rebel security sources in Goma say the situation may deteriorate if militiamen who had fled further into Zaire returned to the area.
"We suspect that some of the Interahamwe are trying to get back to build up a stronghold -- and that will have to be dealt with," said one rebel officer.

Ethnic war has haunted the hilly Masisi region west of Goma for generations, not only between Hutus and Tutsis whose roots lie in Rwanda and Burundi, but also between other tribes who say that only they are truly Zairean.
